newsitem.title: USA: U.S. beef industry rolls out new ad campaign.
newsitem.headline: U.S. beef industry rolls out new ad campaign.

text.p: The beef industry wants Americans to stop playing hard to get with their dinner.
Certain that Americans crave beef but just won't admit it, the beef industry launched an advertising campaign Tuesday with the slogan, "Beef. It's What You Want."

"Our research showed that consumers have strong emotional attachments to beef, unlike any other meat," said Monica Eorgoff, marketing director at the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, which represents cattle producers.
The $13.5 million ad campaign, which starts Aug. 4 and runs through the fall of 1998, features four 30-second television ads.

One spot shows a man dashing to the supermarket to get a steak for his last supper after he sights a fiery meteor headed for Earth. Another shows diners in a restaurant staring lovingly at steak on a nearby plate and the voiceover: "You can see all the longing in an evening without watching TV."

"These ads get to the emotional level of eating beef while our previous campaign focused on the functional aspect of meal planning and preparation," said Eorgoff, referring to the industry's last catch phrase: "Beef. It's What's For Dinner."

U.S. beef producers, who have watched their market share steadily erode to chicken and turkey over the past two decades, are eager to see their so-called "desire strategy" pay off. Beef has lost 11.9 percent of its market share since 1980 and it has cost the industry $12.8 billion, the cattlemen said.
Beef producers readily admit the chicken industry has outdone them in terms of catering to consumers who have little time to cook with convenient packaging and prepped or ready-to-eat products.

"We've simply been trying to force through the system our product in the same form that its been for 30 to 40 years and the market has walked away from us," said John Huston, another marketing executive at the cattlemen's group.

Huston told reporters at a news conference held to announce the ad campaign that the industry was also launching a new marketing strategy to develop and promote prepared beef products like pre-cooked pot roasts.

The beef industry is particularly focused on the chuck and round cuts of meat, which are less tender and take longer to cook, but make up 53 percent of the cow. While steak prices have risen in the past five years, round and chuck have lost about 20 percent of their value.
The cattlemen also plan to follow in the footsteps of the chicken industry by introducing brand-name products for which consumers would pay a premium.
"We're trying to find different ways and angles to beat up on chicken in the marketplace," said Chandler Keys, head of the trade group's Washington office.
The beef producers said they hope to hollow out the decline in market share and start to see an increase by 2005.
